content: Bearberry refers to three species of dwarf shrubs within the genus Arctostaphylos. Unlike other species in this genus, such as Manzanita, bearberries are specifically adapted to arctic and sub-arctic climates. They are distributed across circumpolar regions in northern North America, Asia, and Europe, with one species having a small, isolated population in Central America. The name bearberry originates from the plant's edible fruit, which is reportedly a favorite food of bears. These fruits, also called bearberries, are edible and are sometimes harvested for human consumption. The leaves of the plant are also utilized in herbal medicine. Alpine Bearberry (Arctostaphylos alpina) This species is a low-growing shrub, reaching heights of 10–30 cm. Its leaves are not evergreen, but dead leaves remain attached to the stems for several years. The berries are dark purple to black in color. The plant has a circumpolar distribution, occurring at high latitudes from Scotland across Scandinavia, Russia, Alaska, Canada, and Greenland. Its southern range in Europe includes the Pyrenees and the Alps, while in Asia, it extends to the Altay Mountains. In North America, it is found as far west as British Columbia and as far east as Maine and New Hampshire. Red Bearberry (Arctostaphylos rubra) This species is also a low-growing shrub, reaching heights of 10–30 cm. Its leaves are deciduous, falling in autumn and leaving the stems bare. The berries are red in color. The plant is distributed in mountainous regions of Sichuan in southwestern China, extending north and east to eastern Siberia, Alaska, and northern Canada, reaching as far east as northern Quebec. Common Bearberry (Arctostaphylos uva-ursi) This species is known by various names, including Arberry, Bear’s Grape, Crowberry, Foxberry, Hog Cranberry, Kinnikinnick, Mealberry, Mountain Box, Mountain Cranberry, Mountain Tobacco, Red Bearberry, Sandberry, Upland Cranberry, and Uva-ursi. Medicinal Uses Bearberry leaves contain a variety of bioactive compounds, including arbutin, methylarbutin, ursolic acid, tannic acid, gallic acid, hydroquinones (primarily arbutin, up to 17%), tannins (up to 15%), phenolic glycosides, flavonoids, essential oils, and resin. The leaves are harvested during the summer and dried for use in infusions, liquid extracts, medicinal tea bags, and tablets. The plant is claimed to have numerous medicinal properties, including anti-lithic, aromatic, astringent, disinfectant, diuretic, lithontripic, sedative (renal), mild stimulant, tonic, and urinary antiseptic effects. It has been used to treat a wide range of conditions, including arthritis, lower back pain, bedwetting, bile disorders, bladder infections, bloating, Bright’s disease, bronchitis, bladder catarrh, cystitis, diabetes (by reducing excessive blood sugar), diarrhea, fevers, fluid retention, gallstones, gonorrhea, headaches (when smoked), hemorrhoids, indigestion, kidney stones, kidney infections, liver problems, lung congestion, excessive menstruation, nephritis, obesity, pancreatitis, prostate gland weakness, rheumatism, chronic urethritis, vaginal discharge, vaginal diseases, and water retention. Bearberry is also believed to strengthen the heart muscle and urinary tract, help the uterus return to its normal size after childbirth, and prevent uterine infections. It is claimed to act as a powerful tonic for the bladder’s sphincter muscle, aiding in bladder control issues. Additionally, it exhibits strong bacteriostatic activity against Staphylococcus and Escherichia coli. The leaves possess potent astringent properties. While bearberry is generally considered safe, excessive doses can lead to adverse effects such as nausea, green urine, bluish-gray skin, vomiting, fever, chills, severe back pain, and ringing in the ears. Some individuals can tolerate up to 20 grams, while others may experience toxicity at doses as low as 1 gram. It is recommended not to use bearberry for more than 7–10 days at a time. It is contraindicated in pregnant or breastfeeding individuals, children under 12 years of age, and patients with kidney disease. Drug interactions have been reported with diuretics and medications that acidify the urine, such as ascorbic acid and Urex. History and Folklore Bearberry was first documented in The Physicians of Myddfai, a 13th-century Welsh herbal. It was later described by Clusius in 1601 and recommended for medicinal use in 1763 by Gerhard and others. The plant is often referred to as uva-ursi, derived from the Latin words uva (grape or berry) and ursi (bear), meaning bear’s grape. It was first included in the London Pharmacopoeia in 1788, though its use likely predates this. In Strathnairn, Scotland, there is a hill known in Scottish Gaelic as Cnoc nan Cnàimhseag, meaning The Hill of the Bearberries. Marco Polo reported in the 13th century that the Chinese used bearberry as a diuretic to treat kidney and urinary problems. Bearberry leaves continue to be used medicinally in Poland and other countries. Native Americans incorporated bearberry into their cultural and medicinal practices. It was mixed with tobacco and other herbs for use in religious ceremonies, either as a smudge (a type of incense) or smoked in a sacred pipe to carry prayers to the Great Spirit. When combined with tobacco, it was called Kinnikinnick, an Algonquian word meaning mixture. Native Americans also used bearberry tea to treat urinary tract inflammation, urethritis, kidney stones, and cystitis. The Cheyenne used the tea to treat back sprains, while other tribes powdered the leaves and applied them to sores. Some tribes consumed the tea to address venereal diseases. The berries were also brewed into a tea believed to combat obesity. Early European settlers in the Americas adopted the use of bearberry leaves internally as an astringent to treat nephritis, kidney stones, and other urinary system disorders.
